content.p: Ashfaqulla Khan was hanged at Faizabad jail on 19 December 1927. He was 27. A Muslim from a Pathan family in Shahjahanpur, he had taken part in a train robbery two years earlier, the Kakori action of 9 August 1925, which a group of armed revolutionaries carried out to pay for weapons. A court sentenced him to death along with three other men, among them his friend Ram Prasad Bismil, a Hindu poet and member of the Arya Samaj. Bismil went to the gallows the same morning in a different jail.

The British government labelled him a terrorist, according to Maps of India. In India he is remembered as a martyr, and also as a poet and as half of a friendship that crossed religious lines. The accounts agree on the outline of his story and disagree on many of its dates, which are given below with who says what.

Khan was born on 22 October 1900 in Shahjahanpur, in what is now Uttar Pradesh. Maps of India says he was the youngest of six children of Shafiqur Rahman and Mazharunissa, and that his father worked in the police department. His grandson, Ashfaq Ullah Khan, told The Hindu that the family was rich and well placed, like other Pathans in Shahjahanpur, and that Khan's father was a kotwal, a local police officer.

He wrote Urdu poetry under the pen names Hasrat and Warsi, according to Curious Indian, a popular history site, which also says that he dreamed of opening a school one day. He was at school when Mahatma Gandhi launched the Non-Cooperation Movement, and Maps of India says it shaped him. In February 1922 a crowd of non-cooperation protesters clashed with police at Chauri Chaura in Gorakhpur, and about 22 policemen were killed, according to The Indian Express. Gandhi, opposed to violence, called the movement off. The Express, citing a Press Information Bureau release, says many young Indians were deeply disappointed and that Khan was one of them. After that, it says, he joined the revolutionaries and came to know Bismil.

Bismil was a well-known revolutionary in Shahjahanpur and, according to Maps of India, a member of the Arya Samaj. Accounts of how the two men became friends vary. India Today says Khan's elder brother often spoke to him about Bismil and his poetry, and that the two shared a wish for a united India. Curious Indian says Khan admired Bismil's poems before he met the man.

His grandson told The Hindu a different side of it: that Bismil was at first reluctant to take Khan into the Hindustan Republican Association, because Khan's father was a kotwal. According to the grandson, Bismil later said Khan came under a lot of pressure to disown him and never gave way. Bismil's own grandnephew, Raj Bahadur Tomar, told the same newspaper that the two lived and worked together, and that in the same room Bismil would perform a havan while Khan offered namaz. Tomar presented that as something people say, not something he witnessed.

Pages disagree about who created the Association. IndiaOnline names Shachindra Nath Sanyal as its founder. The Indian National Congress's tribute page says Khan formed it in 1924 with like-minded fighters. The Indian Express says Khan and Bismil founded the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association, the later name, in the mid-1920s. The Express quotes its 1925 manifesto, "The Revolutionary", which aimed at "a federal Republic of United State of India by an organized and armed revolution". The same document declared that Indian revolutionaries "are neither terrorists nor anarchists", although it added that they might at times use terror "as a very effective means of retaliation".

The Association needed money for arms. IndiaOnline and Maps of India both say the members met in Shahjahanpur on 8 August 1925 and decided to rob the government cash that travelled on the Number 8 Down passenger train from Saharanpur to Lucknow. Byju's says the plan was Bismil's and Khan's. On 9 August the train was stopped near Kakori, a town about 16 kilometres from Lucknow, according to Byju's. GKToday and Byju's both say the raiders took about Rs 8,000 from the guard's cabin and did not rob passengers.

The lists of those who took part differ slightly in spelling but agree on the core group. Byju's names ten men in the raiding party, Khan and Bismil among them, along with Azad and Lahiri. Maps of India's list of ten also includes Thakur Roshan Singh. India Today notes a claim that Roshan Singh "was not involved in Kakori but was hanged anyway", and says only that "it is said", without naming who says it.

A passenger, Ahmed Ali, was killed in the exchange of fire, according to GKToday and Byju's, and Byju's says this turned the affair into a case of manslaughter. Curious Indian calls it a stray bullet, and says the death made the case far more serious. Shortly after the robbery, according to IndiaOnline, the government brought in Scotland Yard to investigate, and within a month CID detectives had enough clues to begin making arrests.

Pages give Bismil's arrest as the morning of 26 September 1925, among them IndiaOnline, Maps of India and Byju's. The Indian Express puts it in September 1926, which does not fit with the other pages. Khan was not among those picked up in Shahjahanpur. He went into hiding, and the Express, citing the Press Information Bureau, says he lay low for a time in a sugarcane field half a mile from his home before leaving for Bihar and then Delhi.

IndiaOnline, Maps of India and the Congress page all say he moved between Banaras and Bihar (Maps of India reverses the order) and worked for an engineering company for about ten months. Curious Indian says he hid in Kanpur, moved to Bihar under a changed name, worked quietly as a clerk and learned to speak Bengali. Several pages say he wanted to leave the country, and Maps of India says he hoped to study engineering abroad, because that would help the struggle.

What happened next is told the same way almost everywhere. He went to Delhi and trusted a Pathan friend, who gave him away. The Congress page says this man had been his classmate. Curious Indian says he was an old friend from his home town and that Khan stayed with him. The date of the arrest is where the pages split. The Congress page says police came to his house on the morning of 17 July 1926. Curious Indian says he was arrested in Delhi on 7 December 1926. The Indian Muslim Archive says only "late 1926". Byju's timeline says mid-1926, but also says it came after the trial ended, although the same page has the trial starting in May 1926, so that wording cannot be taken at face value.

IndiaOnline says he was held in "Faridabad jail", which looks like a slip, since Maps of India says Faizabad jail and every page that gives the place of execution names Faizabad. Maps of India says his brother, Riyasatullah, was his counsel.

The Kakori trial began on 21 May 1926 before the sessions court of A. Hamilton, with 28 accused, according to Byju's and GKToday. About 40 people were arrested in all, say Byju's and India Today. Byju's reports that about 15 were let off by the court for lack of evidence. Vajiram and Ravi says the trial lasted about a year and a half, as does The Indian Express.

The Crown's lawyer was Pandit Jagat Narayan Mulla, who, according to Byju's, had refused to defend the accused. The defence names also vary. A separate Byju's page lists Govind Ballabh Pant and Mohan Lal Saxena among the counsel. Curious Indian says Jawaharlal Nehru was on the team as well, and Pant as part of the defence. GKToday says that Bismil represented himself.

Indian Express and Byju's disagree on when the verdict came. Byju's and GKToday say July 1927. The Express says April 1927. They agree on the result. Bismil, Khan, Lahiri and Roshan Singh were sentenced to death. Byju's lists others who were deported to the Cellular Jail at Port Blair or sent to prison: five men got ten years, two got seven years and two got five. India Today alone says five men were given death sentences, adding the name of Swaran Singh, a figure it describes as Bhagat Singh's uncle. No other page opened lists a fifth death sentence, so it is treated here as an error or a different outcome and not as settled.

Curious Indian tells the story that has made Khan a symbol of loyalty. A police officer, it says, walked into his cell and offered him freedom if he would speak against his closest friend in court. He refused, and the site says that this refusal meant he would hang. It names no officer and gives no date, and it is a retelling on a popular site and not a court record.
IndiaOnline says something related. Tasadduk Husain, the superintendent of police, tried to play communal politics between Bismil and Khan and failed. Neither page says what exactly was said.

Byju's says there was a loud outcry in India after the verdict. In a petition to the Viceroy, 78 members of the Central Legislative Assembly asked him to commute the death sentences to life, and the Privy Council and the British king were also approached, without result. Curious Indian adds that Madan Mohan Malaviya personally begged the Viceroy to spare Khan's life and was refused. Byju's says that after sentencing, the prisoners, sent to different jails, went on hunger strike for the treatment of political prisoners.

The executions came between 17 and 19 December 1927, according to Byju's. Lahiri was hanged at Gonda district jail on 17 December, two days ahead of the date set. On the 19th, Bismil was hanged at Gorakhpur, Roshan Singh at Naini jail in Allahabad and Khan at Faizabad.

The accounts of his last moments are brief and differ. IndiaOnline says he kissed the rope and recited the Shahada, the Muslim declaration of faith. The Indian Muslim Archive says he recited verses of the Quran as he died. Curious Indian stresses that Bismil, his closest friend, was hanged that same morning in a different jail. He had written poetry from his cell, the Archive says, under the name Hasrat. His grandson told The Hindu that Khan wrote, in lines like Bismil's poem on being reborn, that as a Muslim he could not speak of rebirth, but that if he met the Almighty he would ask to be born again in India instead of paradise.

Azad, who was never captured, reorganised the Association and ran it until 1931, according to Byju's. He shot himself on 27 February 1931 at Alfred Park (now Chandrashekhar Azad Park) after being badly wounded in a gunfight with police.

The state has since given Khan's name to public projects. In January 2020 the Uttar Pradesh cabinet approved Rs 234 crore for a zoological garden of 121 acres in Gorakhpur, to be named for him, according to The Indian Express. He is also a character in the 2006 film Rang De Basanti, played by Kunal Kapoor, and IndiaOnline and the Express both note it. The Hindu reports that a memorial to Bismil stands in Shahjahanpur, where locals gather on 11 June and 19 December.

The 90th anniversary of the hangings in 2017 was marked by India Today with the line that the main fighters were hanged for a train robbery that holds a prominent place in the history of Indian independence. Khan's grandson told The Hindu that he hoped the story of his grandfather and Bismil would be shown as an example of friendship based on shared ideals.
